nameStory: The Sooty Tern gets its name from its dark, smoky-colored back and wings that look like they've been dusted with soot from an old chimney. The word 'sooty' perfectly captures that charcoal-gray to blackish coloring that covers much of this seabird's upper body, contrasting sharply with its clean white underparts.
description: The Sooty Tern is a medium-sized seabird with striking black and white plumage that spends most of its life soaring over tropical oceans. These remarkable birds have long, pointed wings built for endless flight, and can actually stay airborne for years at a time without landing. They're about the size of a small gull, with a sleek, streamlined body perfect for skimming just above the ocean waves. In New England, they're extremely rare visitors, usually blown in by tropical storms or hurricanes.

idTips.label: Black and white pattern
idTips.description: Sharp contrast between sooty-black upperparts and brilliant white underparts, with a distinctive white forehead patch that looks like a headband against the black cap

idTips.label: Wing shape
idTips.description: Very long, narrow, pointed wings that appear almost crescent-shaped in flight, built for effortless gliding over ocean swells

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Deeply forked black tail that streams behind like scissor blades, often twisted and adjusted during flight maneuvers

idTips.label: Bill
idTips.description: Straight, pointed black bill that looks sharp and dagger-like, perfect for snatching fish and squid from the water surface

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Flies with graceful, buoyant wingbeats interspersed with long glides, rarely flapping rapidly like gulls do

habitat: In New England, Sooty Terns are only seen as extremely rare storm-blown vagrants, typically appearing along the immediate coastline after major hurricanes or tropical storms push them far north of their usual range. When they do appear, look for them resting on beaches, rocky shores, or flying weakly just offshore, often exhausted from their unexpected journey.

seasonality.spring: Virtually never seen in New England during spring, as these birds are breeding on tropical islands thousands of miles south.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare summer vagrant, occasionally appearing after tropical storms. Any sighting would be highly unusual and noteworthy.
seasonality.fall: Most likely season for New England sightings, when hurricanes or major storms can blow these tropical seabirds far north of their normal range.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England winters, as these birds remain in warm tropical waters year-round except when displaced by storms.

funFact: Sooty Terns can fly continuously for 3-10 years without ever touching land, sleeping on the wing by shutting down half their brain at a time while the other half keeps them airborne and alert to danger.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark-backed terns, but the Sooty Tern's crisp black and white pattern with that distinctive white forehead 'headband' is unique. Remember: 'Sooty but not gloomy' - despite the dark back, the bright white forehead and underparts make it look quite striking, not dull.
contextualKnowledge: While called a 'tern,' Sooty Terns behave quite differently from the familiar terns we see in New England - they almost never dive into water like Common or Least Terns do, instead picking food from the ocean surface while barely getting wet.
compareHints: The Sooty Tern differs from its close relative, the Bridled Tern, by having a completely black back (versus brownish-gray) and a broader white forehead patch that extends behind the eye. Bridled Terns also have a white collar that wraps around the back of the neck, which Sooty Terns lack entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Sooty Tern, the Bridled Tern has more muted gray-brown upperparts rather than stark black, and that crucial white forehead patch that extends above the eye.
